faqs.q: What venomous snakes live around Pensacola homes?
faqs.a: All six of Florida's venomous species occur in the Panhandle — the statewide four (cottonmouth, eastern diamondback, dusky pygmy, coralsnake) plus the two northern additions, southern copperhead in leaf-littered hammock edges and timber rattlesnake in the pine woods north of town. In practice, most Pensacola yard snakes are harmless black racers, corn ratsnakes, and gray ratsnakes. Photograph from distance, never handle, and let us identify — a ratsnake in the garage is rodent control you want to keep, while a cottonmouth by the bayou steps is a removal call.

Pensacola.wildlife_intro:
Pensacola layers a 450-year-old downtown — North Hill and East Hill historic homes under ancient oaks — over bayou neighborhoods, NAS Pensacola's southern shore, and suburbs spreading north to Ensley and Ferry Pass. The Panhandle cast differs from peninsular Florida: gray squirrels and raccoons still lead, but this is six-venomous-snake country, skunks are common, flying squirrels slip into attics through gaps no bigger than a quarter, and armadillos dig the red-clay-and-sand yards. Bayou Chico and Bayou Texar pull marsh wildlife into the middle of town.

North Florida has seasons, and Pensacola attics show it — winter cold snaps drive rodents and squirrels inside harder than in Miami, and spring litters in chimneys follow a real calendar. Our bat work names the local trio honestly: Brazilian free-tailed and evening bats, with big brown bats a genuine possibility this far north. Exclusion still obeys the same Florida window, August 15 to April 15, and copperhead and timber rattlesnake identification is part of snake calls here in a way it never is downstate.

Pensacola Beach.wildlife_intro:
Pensacola Beach occupies Santa Rosa Island's western end in Escambia County — a narrow strip of Gulf-front condos, beach houses on pilings, and the quiet neighborhoods around Fort Pickens' national seashore lands. Island wildlife is a short list done thoroughly: roof rats in the condo stacks and beach houses, raccoons in the dumpsters and under raised homes, ghost crabs and shorebirds outside anyone's jurisdiction, and sea turtles nesting on the Gulf side under strict protection. The Sound side adds marsh birds and the occasional otter.

Raised construction is the beach's defining job — everything lives under a piling house if the skirting is open, and storm repairs that never got finished leave the gaps. We seal with stainless materials rated for direct Gulf exposure. For condo buildings, we coordinate with associations on stack-by-stack inspections. No one may touch a turtle nest or a protected shorebird colony, and we flag those for the seashore staff rather than treating them as service items.

faqs.q: How much does wildlife removal cost in Century?

faqs.q: Are copperheads really in the Century area?
faqs.a: Yes — Century sits in the southern copperhead's Florida range, which covers the Panhandle's river bluffs and hammock edges, and timber rattlesnakes also occur in the pine woods of northern Escambia. Both are shy, camouflaged, and most often encountered in leaf litter, woodpiles, and brush piles. Keep those pulled away from the house, wear boots in the bottomland, and photograph any snake from a distance for identification rather than approaching it. A confirmed venomous snake in a yard or woodpile by the house is a legitimate removal call; a ratsnake in the same pile is doing you a favor.

faqs.q: We just moved into a new Cantonment home — why are there rats already?
faqs.a: Because the rats were there first, and the new roofline came with doors. Cleared-flatwoods lots hold roof rats and field rodents that simply move into the new structure through unsealed roof returns and utility penetrations, especially once bird feeders and pet food appear. The fix is a one-time gap audit and seal, plus trimming the palm and shrub contact, rather than a standing poison program — our trapping-and-exclusion approach handles the animals present and closes the building so the next litter grows up somewhere else.

New subdivisions here fool owners twice — first that new means sealed, then that one trapped raccoon ends it. Our Cantonment inspections audit the whole builder package: unsealed roof returns, open soffit corners, garage-door gaps. We seal the pattern, not just the incident. Bats occasionally claim the two-story gables in winter; those get identified and scheduled into the legal exclusion season, August 15 to April 15, with the maternity blackout respected.

faqs.a: Trap the current tenants, then bury the welcome mat. Striped skunks den under porches for the shelter and the grubs in the lawn nearby. Gonzalez.wildlife_intro:
Gonzalez is a small unincorporated community north of Pensacola — rural roads, horse properties, and homes on acreage among the pines, close to the Escambia River's western bluffs. Life here is land-based, and so are the calls: raccoons in barns, skunks under porches, armadillos tearing pastures' edges, moles tunneling the yards, and snakes along the creek bottoms. Residents know their wildlife; they call when an animal moves into a structure, not when one crosses the field.

We respect that line in Gonzalez. Our work is the house, the barn, and the porch — trapping and exclusion where animals have taken up residence — not clearing wildlife from land where it belongs. Porch and deck skirting, feed-room hardening, and chimney caps solve most Gonzalez problems permanently. Any trapped native is released on your land or nearby within Escambia County under the 40-acre written-permission rule, inside the 24-hour window the law sets.

faqs.q: How much does wildlife removal cost in Warrington?
faqs.a: It depends on the animal, how it got in, and how much sealing and cleanup the home needs afterward. Our crew inspects first, shows you the entry points we found, and gives you a quote after inspection before any removal or sealing work begins, with no prices promised over the phone.

faqs.q: Can you relocate a raccoon from my Warrington attic?
faqs.a: Only on Florida's strict conditions. Under FWC Rule 68A-9.010, a live-captured native animal must be released or handled within 24 hours, and an off-site release is lawful only within the same county, on 40 or more contiguous acres, with the release landowner's written permission — or it can be released on-site once the home is sealed. Raccoons are Florida's most-reported rabies carrier, so we never promise a casual drop-off in the woods, and nonnative animals such as iguanas and Muscovy ducks may never be relocated at all.

In Warrington, our crew's steady calls are raccoons in attics and chimneys, eastern gray squirrels at soffits and gable vents, and roof rats moving from palms and fruit trees onto rooflines. Opossums and striped skunks work yards after dark, armadillos dig lawns and beds, eastern moles tunnel the sandy ground, and Brazilian free-tailed and evening bats roost in older rooflines through the warm months. The county's habitat — historic Pensacola, bay and beach communities, and rural north county — and features such as Pensacola Bay, Escambia River, Perdido Bay, Gulf Islands National Seashore keep that pressure close to housing in every season.

Florida has no winter shutdown for this work, so Warrington jobs run year-round, with the one hard legal gate being bats: exclusion is legal only from August 15 through April 15, and maternity-season bat calls become inspection and scheduling. Our crew works under FWC Rule 68A-9.010 with the property owner's authorization — Florida issues no nuisance-trapper license — checks any live trap at least every 24 hours, and seals the entry as part of the job so the next animal cannot use the same opening.
